title: SKEWERSSKEWERSSKEWERS
reviewNotes: Montages, captions and native complete diagrams reviewed. Selected twelve-piece mating variation only, after the queen retreats to g8 near 97 seconds: White Kg3/Rd6/Bc1/c4/e2/f3/h4 against Ke5/Qg8/d7/g4/h5. Native29–31 confirm Bf4+/Kf5/e4 mate with the queen on g8, and native32 confirms the complete earlier piece arrangement with the queen on b8 before the source resets to Qf8. Bf4+ forces Kf5; e4# is actual mate. This does not prove every queen defense to the earlier rook sacrifice loses or certify the larger bishop ending after the main Qf8/Bb2+/Kxd6/Ba3+/Ke6/Bxf8 skewer. The previous full legal reconstruction remains preserved.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only the king of skewers would be able to win from this position. You see, white is left with a rook and a bishop against a queen, and in most situations the queen would be able to overpower these two pieces. [music] But white has an incredible resource in this position. Of course, we start with F6, now attacking the king. And of course, if the queen decides to take, this is going to be a winning end game for white because there is a passed pawn. And if the king goes up, there is simply going to be a discovered check picking up the queen and winning the game. But black is not that naive, and he's simply going to go down to E5. And now white has to find an ingenious move to keep this position alive. And the move is bishop to C1. A brilliant sacrifice that cannot be accepted because of course, if the queen decides to take the rook, [music] there is going to be a skewer picking up the queen and winning the game. And exactly the same happens if the king takes, but that is far from the only problem. You see, if black plays a waiting move in [music] this position, there is going to be bishop to B2 with a checkmate. So black has to defend B2 like this. And now it seems like black is simply out of the woods. The checkmate threat has been stopped, and the king of skewer has no follow up. But that could not be farther from the truth because in this position, the king of skewers plays the brilliant, the majestic and beautiful rook takes D6. Another brilliant sacrifice, and the idea is exactly the same one. This [music] piece cannot be taken by either the king or the queen because there is going to be a bishop skewer picking up the queen like this. And not only that, white is again threatening a checkmate. For example, if the queen moves here, there is going to be bishop to F4 followed up by E4 [music] with a checkmate. So black has no other choice but to defend the F4 square with the queen, and he is still confident that the queen is eventually going to win. But white is not done with the skewers and with the brilliant sacrifices. And he follows up with the only move, the precise bishop B2 check. The king doesn't have many squares to go to apart from this one or taking the rook. But if the king goes here, there's simply going to be a fork attacking the king and the queen defended by the bishop. And finally, if the king takes the rook, there is going [music] to be yet again one last skewer attacking the king and queen and securing the win for white. If you love incredible chess, follow for more.
